title: Xevious
description: Xevious, Namco's 1982 vertical scrolling shooter, set the template for the genre: the player flies a Solvalou fighter over scrolling terrain, firing at air targets while bombing ground targets with a separate sight. The terrain scrolls continuously beneath the ship, and the game's mix of air and ground combat, plus its hidden towers and flags, gave it unusual depth.
body:
Xevious, Namco's 1982 vertical scrolling shooter, set the template for the genre: the player flies a Solvalou fighter over scrolling terrain, firing at air targets while bombing ground targets with a separate sight. The terrain scrolls continuously beneath the ship, and the game's mix of air and ground combat, plus its hidden towers and flags, gave it unusual depth.

The tribute demo flies a scrolling course starting on row 2, with enemies spawning on ticks 2, 6, 10, 14: the player moves between rows and shoots, surviving the scroll while picking off enemies before they reach the ship. It is an original miniature inspired by the scrolling-shooter idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

The bomb sight leads the ship, so ground targets must be bombed before they pass under the fighter, not as they arrive. Air targets are best met with short bursts, since the fighter's fire is narrow and the sky fills quickly.
controls: Type up/down/left/right/shoot each tick to survive the scroll, quit to stop.

description: 1942, Capcom's 1984 vertical shooter, puts the player in a World War II fighter plane over the Pacific, dodging and shooting waves of enemy aircraft. The game introduced the loop maneuver, a barrel roll that clears bullets and enemies around the plane, and its escalating waves made it a defining arcade shooter.
body:
1942, Capcom's 1984 vertical shooter, puts the player in a World War II fighter plane over the Pacific, dodging and shooting waves of enemy aircraft. The game introduced the loop maneuver, a barrel roll that clears bullets and enemies around the plane, and its escalating waves made it a defining arcade shooter.

The tribute demo flies a scrolling course starting on row 3, with enemies spawning on ticks 1, 5, 9, 13, 17: the player moves between rows and shoots, surviving the scroll while picking off enemies before they reach the ship. It is an original miniature inspired by the scrolling-shooter idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

The loop is a defensive tool, not an attack: it should be saved for moments when bullets box the plane in, since it has a cooldown. Enemy formations arrive in recognizable patterns, so learning the wave order predicts where the next squadron appears.
controls: Type up/down/left/right/shoot each tick to survive the scroll, quit to stop.

description: Raiden, Seibu Kaihatsu's 1990 vertical shooter, is known for its punishing bullet patterns, its wide arsenal of weapons, and its two-player cooperative play. The player's fighter collects weapon icons that upgrade its main gun and missiles, and the game rewards precise dodging through dense bullet curtains.
body:
Raiden, Seibu Kaihatsu's 1990 vertical shooter, is known for its punishing bullet patterns, its wide arsenal of weapons, and its two-player cooperative play. The player's fighter collects weapon icons that upgrade its main gun and missiles, and the game rewards precise dodging through dense bullet curtains.

Bullet curtains reward small movements: the fighter's hitbox is smaller than its sprite, so threading gaps beats sweeping dodges. Weapon icons should be collected deliberately, since switching weapons mid-stage can downgrade a favored gun.

The charge shot builds while the player holds fire, so the best rhythm is to hold fire through calm stretches and release on armored targets. Naval targets on the sea surface should be strafed in passes, not hovered over, since their return fire tracks a stationary plane.

body:
Strikers 1945, Psikyo's 1995 vertical shooter, is a World War II-themed shooter with six selectable planes, each with its own shot pattern and bomb. The game is known for its fast bullets, its gold-bar scoring system, and its randomly ordered stages that keep runs fresh.

The tribute demo flies a scrolling course starting on row 3, with enemies spawning on ticks 1, 5, 9, 13, 17: the player moves between rows and shoots, surviving the scroll while picking off enemies before they reach the ship. It is an original miniature inspired by the scrolling-shooter idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

Gold bars appear from destroyed ground targets and multiply the score when collected in chains, so the player should sweep ground targets before air targets on each pass. Random stage order means no run is identical, so adaptability beats memorized routes.

title: DoDonPachi
description: DoDonPachi, Cave's 1997 vertical shooter, is a landmark bullet-hell game where the screen fills with dense, patterned bullet curtains and the player threads a tiny hitbox through gaps. Its chaining system rewards destroying enemies in quick succession, and its difficulty set a new bar for the genre.
body:
DoDonPachi, Cave's 1997 vertical shooter, is a landmark bullet-hell game where the screen fills with dense, patterned bullet curtains and the player threads a tiny hitbox through gaps. Its chaining system rewards destroying enemies in quick succession, and its difficulty set a new bar for the genre.

The tribute demo flies a scrolling course starting on row 2, with enemies spawning on ticks 3, 7, 11, 15, 19: the player moves between rows and shoots, surviving the scroll while picking off enemies before they reach the ship. It is an original miniature inspired by the scrolling-shooter idea, not a copy of the arcade game.

Bullet-hell play is about the hitbox, not the sprite: the ship's vulnerable point is far smaller than its artwork, so gaps that look impossible are often passable. Chaining rewards continuous destruction, so the player should keep firing even while dodging, never letting the chain timer lapse.
controls: Type up/down/left/right/shoot each tick to survive the scroll, quit to stop.
